package_info.package_manager: N/A (custom malware, not distributed via public package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: FritzFrog is a custom-built, fileless, peer-to-peer (P2P) botnet written in Go that targets SSH servers. It operates entirely in memory, spreading laterally by brute-forcing SSH credentials, establishing a decentralized encrypted P2P network for command and control, and deploying a Monero cryptominer. Its fileless, decentralized nature, unauthorized cryptomining, and ability to propagate without leaving artifacts on disk make it inherently malicious and difficult to detect.

execution_context.file_location: memory (fileless, loaded directly after SSH compromise; no persistent files on disk)
required_permissions: network (for P2P communication and lateral movement)
filesystem (to execute cryptominer and potentially modify SSH authorized_keys)
process_execution (to launch cryptominer and maintain persistence)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Custom Go code that, after gaining SSH access, loads the botnet payload directly into memory, establishes encrypted P2P connections with other infected hosts, modifies SSH authorized_keys for persistence, and executes cryptomining operations. The code also scans for additional SSH targets and propagates itself by brute-forcing credentials.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At post-SSH-compromise, the code injects a memory-resident Go binary, establishes encrypted P2P connections with other infected hosts, modifies SSH authorized_keys for persistence, scans for additional SSH servers, brute-forces credentials to propagate, and launches a Monero cryptominer process, all while avoiding disk writes to remain undetected.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code operates entirely in memory, avoids writing files to disk, establishes unauthorized encrypted P2P network connections for decentralized command and control, modifies SSH authorized_keys without user consent, and launches a cryptominer. These behaviors are hallmarks of advanced, evasive malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal SSH server operation does not involve loading arbitrary code into memory, establishing P2P botnet connections, modifying SSH authorized_keys without administrator action, or launching cryptomining processes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: In-memory execution is sometimes used by legitimate security tools for forensics or memory analysis, and SSH authorized_keys may be modified by administrators for access control, but not for persistent, unauthorized network activity or self-propagation.
key_indicators: fileless operation (no malware files on disk despite active malicious processes)
encrypted P2P network traffic on non-standard ports
unexpected in-memory Go processes with no corresponding files
lateral movement via SSH using brute-forced credentials
sustained high CPU usage due to cryptomining

attack_chain.action: Brute-forces SSH credentials to gain unauthorized access to the target server.
attack_chain.leads_to: In-memory deployment of the FritzFrog botnet payload.

attack_chain.action: Loads the botnet code directly into memory, avoiding disk writes, and modifies SSH authorized_keys for persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: Establishes encrypted P2P connections with other infected hosts and maintains access.

attack_chain.action: Joins the decentralized P2P botnet, receives commands, scans for additional SSH targets, propagates via brute-force, and launches a Monero cryptominer.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ongoing cryptomining, lateral movement, and potential for further malicious activity.

behavioral_signatures: fileless malware operation (no persistent files on disk despite active malicious processes)
unexpected outbound encrypted P2P network traffic from SSH servers on non-standard ports
unauthorized modification of SSH authorized_keys file
sudden and sustained increase in CPU usage due to cryptomining processes
lateral movement via SSH using brute-forced credentials
in-memory Go processes with no corresponding executable on disk
file_indicators: absence of malware files on disk despite observed malicious activity
unexpected in-memory Go binaries with no matching file on disk
network_indicators: encrypted P2P traffic on high, non-standard TCP ports (e.g., 12345, 5555, 2222)
outbound connections to multiple external IPs not typical for SSH servers
frequent SSH connection attempts to external hosts (indicative of propagation)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor SSH servers for in-memory Go processes with no corresponding files on disk, unauthorized changes to SSH authorized_keys, and unexpected encrypted P2P network traffic on non-standard ports. Correlate with spikes in CPU usage and failed SSH login attempts. Use EDR and memory forensics tools capable of detecting fileless malware and memory-resident threats. Implement network monitoring to identify anomalous outbound SSH and P2P traffic patterns.
